scope: Perennial vegetables that overwinter in the ground in zone 6b/7a (Annandale, NJ) and are sold by mail: asparagus, rhubarb, horseradish, sunchokes, perennial onions and leeks, skirret, groundnut, crosnes, sea kale, Good King Henry, sorrels, Turkish rocket, perennial kale, sochan, lovage, Caucasian mountain spinach, nettles, fuki, ostrich fern and similar crops. Every form is tracked: live plants, crowns, tubers, root cuttings and seed packets. Named cultivars are listed separately from the plain species, and seed packets are listed separately from plants. Left out: crops that don't survive a zone 6 winter outdoors (yacon, oca, mashua, tree collards, globe artichoke), ordinary annual vegetables, and culinary herbs.

varieties.name: Asparagus

varieties.description: Long-lived crown that sends up spears every spring. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil and harvest lightly from the second or third year. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Crimson Red rhubarb
varieties.summary: Red stalks with a tart-sweet flavor.
varieties.description: Variety with red stalks, popular in the Pacific Northwest. Clump-forming perennial grown for its leaf stalks; the leaf blades are toxic and are thrown away. Likes rich soil and cold winters. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Victoria rhubarb
varieties.summary: Old English variety; green stalks blushed red, vigorous.
varieties.description: Old English variety with green stalks blushed red. Vigorous and reliable. Clump-forming perennial grown for its leaf stalks; the leaf blades are toxic and are thrown away. Likes rich soil and cold winters. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Horseradish
varieties.summary: Pungent root; it spreads, so give it its own corner.
varieties.description: Deep-rooted perennial dug in fall or early spring for its hot roots. Any piece of root left behind regrows, so it is usually given a bed of its own. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Variegated horseradish
varieties.summary: Leaves splashed with cream; roots used as usual.
varieties.description: Form with leaves splashed cream and white. The roots are used like ordinary horseradish. Deep-rooted perennial dug in fall or early spring for its hot roots. Any piece of root left behind regrows, so it is usually given a bed of its own. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Sunchoke
varieties.summary: Tall native sunflower with crisp, nutty tubers dug in fall and winter.
varieties.description: North American sunflower relative, 6 to 10 feet tall, that makes knobby edible tubers. Very productive, and it comes back from any tuber left in the ground. Also sold as Jerusalem artichoke. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Red Fuseau sunchoke
varieties.summary: Smooth, long, red-skinned tubers that are easy to clean.
varieties.description: Variety with smooth, elongated red-skinned tubers and few knobs. North American sunflower relative, 6 to 10 feet tall, that makes knobby edible tubers. Very productive, and it comes back from any tuber left in the ground. Also sold as Jerusalem artichoke. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Stampede sunchoke
varieties.summary: Early white type with large tubers.
varieties.description: Early-maturing white variety suited to short seasons. North American sunflower relative, 6 to 10 feet tall, that makes knobby edible tubers. Very productive, and it comes back from any tuber left in the ground. Also sold as Jerusalem artichoke. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: White Fuseau sunchoke
varieties.summary: Smooth, elongated white tubers.
varieties.description: Variety with smooth, elongated white tubers and few knobs. North American sunflower relative, 6 to 10 feet tall, that makes knobby edible tubers. Very productive, and it comes back from any tuber left in the ground. Also sold as Jerusalem artichoke. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: White Jewel sunchoke
varieties.summary: White-skinned named selection.
varieties.description: White-skinned named selection; see the seller's page for details. North American sunflower relative, 6 to 10 feet tall, that makes knobby edible tubers. Very productive, and it comes back from any tuber left in the ground. Also sold as Jerusalem artichoke. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Walking onion
varieties.summary: Top-setting onion: scallions in spring, small bulbs at the top in summer.
varieties.description: Hardy perennial onion that forms clusters of small bulbs at the top of its stalks, which bend over and replant themselves. Used as green onions and for the small bulbs. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: McCullar's White walking onion
varieties.summary: White-bulbed top-setting onion.
varieties.description: Top-setting onion with white bulbs. Hardy perennial onion that forms clusters of small bulbs at the top of its stalks, which bend over and replant themselves. Used as green onions and for the small bulbs. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Welsh onion
varieties.summary: Perennial bunching onion that divides at the base.
varieties.description: Clump-forming scallion that never makes a large bulb. Cut or divide it and it keeps coming back. Hardy to zone 5 or colder.

varieties.name: Welsh onion seeds
varieties.summary: Seed packet. Perennial bunching onion that divides at the base.
varieties.description: Clump-forming scallion that never makes a large bulb. Cut or divide it and it keeps coming back. Hardy to zone 5 or colder. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: Red Welsh onion
varieties.summary: Welsh onion with red-skinned bases.
varieties.description: Strain of Welsh onion with red-skinned bases. Clump-forming scallion that never makes a large bulb. Cut or divide it and it keeps coming back. Hardy to zone 5 or colder.

varieties.name: Perennial leek
varieties.summary: A leek that multiplies and comes back each year.
varieties.description: Perennial forms of leek that divide at the base or make bulbils. Harvested as slender leeks from fall through spring; most go dormant in summer.

varieties.name: Babington's leek
varieties.summary: Top-setting perennial leek from the British coast.
varieties.description: Wild leek from the coasts of Britain and Ireland that makes a head of bulbils instead of seed. Perennial forms of leek that divide at the base or make bulbils. Harvested as slender leeks from fall through spring; most go dormant in summer.

varieties.name: Potato onion
varieties.summary: Multiplier onion: plant one bulb, harvest a cluster.
varieties.description: Old-fashioned multiplier onion. Each bulb planted in fall or early spring divides into a cluster of bulbs; keep some back to replant.

varieties.name: Bear's garlic
varieties.summary: European woodland wild garlic with broad garlicky leaves in spring.
varieties.description: Shade-loving relative of ramps, also called ramsons. Leaves, flowers and bulbs are eaten, and it goes dormant in summer. Seed needs a cold period and can be slow to sprout. Hardy to about zone 5.

Hardy to about zone 5. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: Garlic chives
varieties.summary: Flat, garlic-flavored leaves from a cut-and-come-again clump.
varieties.description: Clumping perennial with flat leaves and edible white flowers in late summer. It self-sows freely, so deadhead it to keep it in bounds. Hardy to zone 4.

varieties.name: Garlic chives seeds
varieties.summary: Seed packet. Flat, garlic-flavored leaves from a cut-and-come-again clump.

varieties.summary: Broad-leaved giant selection.
varieties.description: Selection with larger, broader leaves than ordinary garlic chives. Clumping perennial with flat leaves and edible white flowers in late summer. It self-sows freely, so deadhead it to keep it in bounds. Hardy to zone 4.

varieties.name: Nodding onion seeds
varieties.summary: Seed packet. Native wild onion with edible leaves, bulbs and pink flowers.
varieties.description: Clumping North American native onion for sun or light shade. All parts are edible with a strong onion flavor. Hardy to zone 4. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: Skirret
varieties.summary: Clusters of sweet, pencil-thick white roots; an old European root crop.
varieties.description: Hardy perennial in the carrot family grown for bundles of sweet roots dug from fall to spring. Replant the crown or offsets to keep the patch going. Likes moist, rich soil. Hardy to about zone 5.

Hardy to about zone 5. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: Groundnut
varieties.summary: Native nitrogen-fixing vine with strings of starchy tubers.
varieties.description: Twining native legume, also called hopniss, that makes chains of protein-rich tubers. Best dug after two seasons. Hardy to zone 4.

varieties.name: Crosnes
varieties.summary: Small, crisp, spiral tubers from a spreading mint relative.
varieties.description: Also called Chinese artichoke or mint root. A spreading groundcover in the mint family; the tubers are dug in late fall and winter. Hardy to zone 5.

varieties.name: Sea kale
varieties.summary: Blue-gray coastal perennial: blanched spring shoots, leaves and broccoli-like buds.
varieties.description: Long-lived cabbage relative. Spring shoots are traditionally blanched under a pot, and the young leaves and flower buds are eaten too. Needs sun and sharp drainage. Hardy to about zone 5.

varieties.name: Homesteader's Kaleidoscopic Perennial kale seeds
varieties.summary: Seed packet. Diverse seed mix for selecting your own perennial kale.
varieties.description: A grex: a deliberately varied seed mix from crosses involving perennial kales. Grow it out, keep the plants that live longest and taste best, and multiply those from cuttings. Perennial forms of kale that keep producing leaves for several years. Named clones are grown from cuttings; seed mixes give varied plants to select from. Winter hardiness varies, so check each seller's zone rating. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: The Next Homesteader's Kaleidoscopic Perennial kale seeds
varieties.summary: Seed packet. Follow-on generation of the Kaleidoscopic grex.
varieties.description: A later generation of the Homesteader's Kaleidoscopic Perennial kale grex, sold as a varied seed mix. Perennial forms of kale that keep producing leaves for several years. Named clones are grown from cuttings; seed mixes give varied plants to select from. Winter hardiness varies, so check each seller's zone rating. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: Sochan
varieties.summary: Native cutleaf coneflower; tender spring greens long eaten by the Cherokee.
varieties.description: Tall native wildflower of moist soils and part shade, 5 to 8 feet in bloom. The young spring leaves are cooked as greens. Spreads by rhizomes. Usually sold as cutleaf or green-headed coneflower. Hardy to zone 3.

Usually sold as cutleaf or green-headed coneflower. Hardy to zone 3. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: Lovage
varieties.summary: Tall celery-flavored perennial; leaves, stalks and seeds are all used.
varieties.description: Grows to 6 feet with a strong celery flavor; one plant is plenty for most kitchens. Hardy to zone 4.

varieties.name: Lovage seeds
varieties.summary: Seed packet. Tall celery-flavored perennial; leaves, stalks and seeds are all used.
varieties.description: Grows to 6 feet with a strong celery flavor; one plant is plenty for most kitchens. Hardy to zone 4. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: Caucasian mountain spinach
varieties.summary: Shade-tolerant climbing perennial spinach.
varieties.description: Climbs 6 to 10 feet each year from a long-lived crown. Very early spring shoots and mild leaves through the season. Hardy to zone 4 or colder.

varieties.name: Caucasian mountain spinach seeds
varieties.summary: Seed packet. Shade-tolerant climbing perennial spinach.
varieties.description: Climbs 6 to 10 feet each year from a long-lived crown. Very early spring shoots and mild leaves through the season. Hardy to zone 4 or colder. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: Stinging nettle
varieties.summary: Spring greens for cooking and tea; it stings until cooked or dried.
varieties.description: Spreading perennial harvested with gloves in spring. Cooking or drying removes the sting. Spreads by rhizomes, so site it away from paths. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Stinging nettle seeds
varieties.summary: Seed packet. Spring greens for cooking and tea; it stings until cooked or dried.
varieties.description: Spreading perennial harvested with gloves in spring. Cooking or drying removes the sting. Spreads by rhizomes, so site it away from paths. Hardy to zone 3. Sold here as seed; plants grown from seed take a year or more to reach harvest size.

varieties.name: Fuki
varieties.summary: Japanese butterbur: a big-leaved shade plant grown for spring stalks and flower buds.
varieties.description: Spreads strongly in moist shade, so plant it where it can be contained. The stalks are parboiled before eating. Hardy to zone 5.

varieties.name: Ostrich fern
varieties.summary: Native fern that gives fiddleheads in spring.
varieties.description: Tall native fern for moist shade. The tightly curled spring fiddleheads are picked and must be cooked before eating. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Earth chestnut
varieties.summary: Carrot-family perennial with small chestnut-flavored tubers.
varieties.description: Makes small rounded tubers with a chestnut-like flavor; the leaves are used like parsley and the seeds as a spice. Hardy to about zone 5.

varieties.name: Wapato
varieties.summary: Native arrowhead for pond edges, with starchy tubers.
varieties.description: Also called duck potato. Grows in shallow water or mud and makes egg-sized tubers in fall. Hardy to zone 3.

varieties.name: Jersey Giant asparagus
varieties.summary: All-male Rutgers hybrid with rust resistance and Fusarium tolerance.
varieties.description: All-male hybrid patented by Rutgers University in 1985, bred in New Jersey. Green spears; in Rutgers trials on Fusarium-infested New Jersey soil it gave about double the marketable yield of Mary Washington. Disease-resistant to rust, with good field tolerance to Fusarium crown and root rot, and widely adapted.
varieties.one_liner: The all-male Rutgers hybrid bred on New Jersey soil

varieties.name: Jersey Supreme asparagus
varieties.summary: Early, high-yielding all-male hybrid with rust resistance.
varieties.description: All-male F1 hybrid from Jersey Asparagus Farms, listed in 2002. Early-ripening, high-yielding green spears of medium to medium-large size, with slightly purple bracts in cool weather. Disease-resistant to rust and adapted to both warm and cool temperate climates.
varieties.one_liner: The early all-male hybrid, about a week ahead of Jersey Knight

varieties.name: Apollo asparagus
varieties.summary: Early, vigorous hybrid with tight purple-tinged tips.
varieties.description: Hybrid from California Asparagus Seed and Transplants. Early-ripening and vigorous, with green spears that taper to a tight head tinged purple at the tip. Disease-resistant to Fusarium and asparagus rust.
varieties.one_liner: The early, vigorous one with rust and Fusarium resistance

varieties.name: Viking asparagus
varieties.summary: Old Canadian selection of Mary Washington with large spears.
varieties.description: Selected from Mary Washington stock at the Horticultural Experiment Station in Vineland, Ontario, and released in 1945. Large, slightly paler green spears on vigorous plants with heavy yields, and considerable resistance to rust. Generally adapted.
varieties.one_liner: The old Ontario selection with big spears and heavy yields

varieties.name: Pacific Purple asparagus
varieties.summary: Sweet, low-fiber purple asparagus from New Zealand.
varieties.description: Purple asparagus bred by Aspara Pacific in New Zealand. Thick purple spears with very high sugar content and low fiber, tender enough to eat raw, and one of the highest-yielding purple types. Sellers report good Fusarium resistance; seed-grown plants include females, so crowns are the usual way to buy it.
varieties.one_liner: The sweet purple one from New Zealand, tender enough to eat raw

varieties.name: Pacific 2000 asparagus
varieties.summary: All-male New Zealand hybrid with tender, stringless green spears.
varieties.description: Vigorous all-male asparagus bred in New Zealand. Thick, upright, uniform mid-green spears, noted for flavor and a tender, stringless texture, with heavy yields. Long-lived crowns take two to five years to reach full production.
varieties.one_liner: The all-male New Zealand green known for tender, stringless spears

varieties.name: Canada Red rhubarb
varieties.summary: Short, slender, very sweet red stalks with few seed stalks.
varieties.description: Red-stalked rhubarb first introduced in Canada and long popular. Stalks are shorter and more slender than most but tender and very sweet, with good red color and few seed stalks.
varieties.one_liner: The sweet red Canadian one that rarely goes to seed

varieties.name: Valentine rhubarb
varieties.summary: Broad, deep red, low-acid stalks that stay rosy when cooked.
varieties.description: Red rhubarb with broad, deep red stalks that keep a rosy color when cooked. Much less acid than green-stalked and many other red varieties, with few or no seed stalks, and good for freezing. Recommended for home gardens by Iowa State.
varieties.one_liner: The low-acid red one that keeps its color in the pie

varieties.name: MacDonald rhubarb
varieties.summary: Productive red rhubarb with tender-skinned, brilliant red stalks.
varieties.description: Red-stalked rhubarb that produces well, with tender skin on brilliant red stalks and excellent flavor. Recommended as a red-stalked choice for home gardens by Iowa State.
varieties.one_liner: The productive one with tender, brilliant red stalks

varieties.name: Cherry Red rhubarb
varieties.summary: Vigorous rhubarb with long, thick stalks red inside and out.
varieties.description: Vigorous rhubarb with long, thick stalks that are rich red inside and out. Juicy and tender; Wisconsin Extension calls it sweet, while other descriptions call it tart.
varieties.one_liner: The big one with stalks red all the way through

varieties.name: Timperley Early rhubarb
varieties.summary: Very early English rhubarb with thick, red-to-green stems.
varieties.description: Old English rhubarb known for very early growth in spring. High-yielding, with thick stems that run from deep red at the base to light green flecked with red.
varieties.one_liner: The very early one for the first rhubarb of spring

varieties.name: Dwarf Sunray sunchoke
varieties.summary: White-tubered type that flowers freely; heavy yields in an Ohio trial.
varieties.description: White-skinned sunchoke that flowers freely and is sold for flower borders as a shorter type, though in an Ohio State trial it reached about 8 feet. In that trial it made the largest average tubers and about 16 lb of tubers per plant, and bloomed from early summer.
varieties.one_liner: The free-flowering white one with big tubers

varieties.name: Jack's Copperclad sunchoke
varieties.summary: Short, slow-growing type with dark red tubers.
varieties.description: Red-skinned sunchoke with a darker red hue than most. In an Ohio State trial it was the shortest and slowest-growing variety, under 4 feet by fall, low-branching and suited to small gardens or containers, with small tubers and a lighter yield.
varieties.one_liner: The short red one for small gardens and containers

varieties.name: Beaver Valley Purple sunchoke
varieties.summary: Red-purple tubers on a mid-height, low-branching plant.
varieties.description: Red-skinned sunchoke passed around by small permaculture farms. In an Ohio State trial it grew to about 6.5 feet, branched low and suited small gardens, bloomed in July, and gave a modest yield of medium tubers.
varieties.one_liner: The mid-height red one for smaller gardens

varieties.name: Clearwater sunchoke
varieties.summary: Long tubers with fewer knobs, easier to clean.
varieties.description: Sunchoke selection with relatively long tubers and fewer knobs than French Mammoth White, making them easier to clean and peel. Like other sunchokes it is very hardy and comes back from tubers left in the ground.
varieties.one_liner: The smoother one that's easier to scrub and peel
